translationRepairs: The Sons of Emperor Wen, Emperor Xiaomin, Emperor Wu, and Emperor Xuan
The Sons of Emperor Wen, Emperor Xiaomin, Emperor Ming, Emperor Wu, and Emperor Xuan
s0001 reads 文閔明武宣諸子; 明 is Emperor Ming and is omitted from the idiomatic English, so inserting Emperor Ming restores the five-reign title.
Princes of Wen, Xiaomin, Wu, and Xuan
Princes of Wen, Xiaomin, Ming, Wu, and Xuan
The same Chinese title lists 明 among five reign shorthand names; the literal must include Ming.
Emperor Wen (Yuwen Tai) had thirteen sons.
s0002 is only 文帝十三子; Yuwen Tai is not in the Chinese and the parenthetical is an invented gloss.
Yuwen Zhi was a younger brother on the emperor's grandmother's side; by nature he was frivolous and deceitful, greedy and ruthless, and unrestrained.
Yuwen Zhi was a uterine younger brother of the High Ancestor; by nature he was frivolous and deceitful, greedy and ruthless, and unrestrained.
直高祖母弟 parses as 高祖 + 母弟 (Gaozu's uterine younger brother), not kinship through a grandmother.
Zhi was the younger brother of the emperor's elder grandmother's line; by nature he was frivolous and deceitful, greedy and ruthless, without restraint.
Zhi was the High Ancestor's younger brother by the same mother; by nature he was frivolous and deceitful, greedy and ruthless, without restraint.
Literal likewise misreads 高祖母弟 as an elder-grandmother line; it means Gaozu's same-mother younger brother.
Before long he showed further treasonous intent; he was executed together with his sons He, Gong, Sai, Xiang, Jia, Mi, Jin, Qianli, Qianbao, Qiancong, and ten others in all; the fief was abolished.
Before long he showed further treasonous intent; he was executed together with his sons He, Gong, Sai, Xiang, Jia, Mi, Jin, Qianli, Qianzao, Qiancong, and ten others in all; the fief was abolished.
The son list includes 乾璪; 璪 is zǎo, so Qianzao is correct and Qianbao is wrong.
Soon he again harbored different intent; he was then executed, together with his sons He, Gong, Sai, Xiang, Jia, Mi, Jin, Qianli, Qianbao, Qiancong, and ten others in all; the state was abolished.
Soon he again harbored different intent; he was then executed, together with his sons He, Gong, Sai, Xiang, Jia, Mi, Jin, Qianli, Qianzao, Qiancong, and ten others in all; the state was abolished.
Literal of the same unit must romanize 乾璪 as Qianzao, not Qianbao.
In the second year, Emperor Xuan was indisposed; Zhao and the five princes of Chen, Yue, Dai, and Teng were summoned to court.
In the second year, Emperor Xuan was indisposed; Zhao and the princes of Chen, Yue, Dai, and Teng—five princes in all—were summoned to court.
招及陳、越、代、滕五王 means Zhao plus Chen, Yue, Dai, and Teng as five princes total; 'the five princes of Chen…' wrongly implies five besides Zhao.
Soon advanced to pillar-of-state; he went out as commander-in-chief of Qinzhou, transferred to Shanzhou, and supervised Yannmen Duke Tian Hong in capturing nine Qi cities including Yiyang.
Soon advanced to pillar-of-state; he went out as commander-in-chief of Qinzhou, transferred to Shanzhou, and supervised Yanmen Duke Tian Hong in capturing nine Qi cities including Yiyang.
督鴈門公田弘 uses 鴈門; the English place/title is Yanmen, and Yannmen is a misspelling.

Soon advanced to pillar-of-state; went out as Qinzhou commander-in-chief, transferred to Shanzhou commander-in-chief, and supervised Yannmen Duke Tian Hong in capturing nine Qi cities including Yiyang.

Soon advanced to pillar-of-state; went out as Qinzhou commander-in-chief, transferred to Shanzhou commander-in-chief, and supervised Yanmen Duke Tian Hong in capturing nine Qi cities including Yiyang.
Literal has the same 鴈門 misspelled as Yannmen; Yanmen is the accurate form.
In the first year of Xuanzheng (578), he entered office as grand minister of war.
In the first year of Xuanzheng (578), he entered office as grand minister of state.
宣政元年，入為大冢宰; 大冢宰 is the chief minister (minister of state/steward), not 大司馬 minister of war.
In the first year of Xuanzheng, he entered office as grand minister of war.
In the first year of Xuanzheng, he entered office as grand minister of state.
Literal of s0212 likewise mistranslates 大冢宰 as minister of war; grand minister of state matches the office.
He then went out as commander-in-chief of Lishi and four other provinces, the defenses of Greater and Lesser Sword, and all related military affairs, and as governor of Li Province.
He then went out as commander-in-chief of Li, Shi, and three other provinces, the defenses of Greater and Lesser Sword, and all related military affairs, and as governor of Li Province.
總管利始等五州 names 利 and 始 as two of five provinces; fusing them as Lishi invents a place-name.
He then went out as commander-in-chief of Lishi and four other provinces, the two defenses of Greater and Lesser Sword, and all military affairs, and governor of Li Province.
He then went out as commander-in-chief of Li, Shi, and three other provinces, the two defenses of Greater and Lesser Sword, and all military affairs, and governor of Li Province.
Literal has the same false fusion of 利始 into Lishi; Li and Shi as two of five provinces is correct.
At the beginning of Daxiang (579), he was grand minister of war.
At the beginning of Daxiang (579), he was grand steward.
大象初，為大冢宰; again 大冢宰 is the grand steward, not minister of war.
He held the offices of senior pillar-of-state, grand minister of war, and grand right assistant.
He held the offices of senior pillar-of-state, grand steward, and grand right assistant.
Office string 上柱國、大冢宰、大右弼 includes 大冢宰 as grand steward, not grand minister of war.
Senior pillar-of-state, grand minister of war, grand right assistant.
Senior pillar-of-state, grand steward, grand right assistant.
Literal of s0263 must render 大冢宰 as grand steward rather than minister of war.
what Jisi (Sima Qian) set forth cannot be applied in the court of accomplished Zhou.
what Jisi (Shusun Tong) set forth cannot be applied in the court of accomplished Zhou.
稷嗣 is the title of Shusun Tong (稷嗣君); identifying Jisi as Sima Qian invents a false attribution.

Had Emperor Xuan adopted the systems of the Zhou founders Ji Fa and Liu Lei, surveyed sage techniques, assigned worthy kin inside and outside the court, gauged their weight, mixed near and distant kin, head and tail supporting each other, far and near each serving a use—

Had Emperor Xuan adopted the systems of Ji and Liu (Zhou and Han), surveyed sage techniques, assigned worthy kin inside and outside the court, gauged their weight, mixed near and distant kin, head and tail supporting each other, far and near each serving a use—
采姬、劉之制 refers to the Ji and Liu institutional models (Zhou and Han), not individuals Ji Fa and Liu Lei.
Kan they were all killed by Yang Jian; their fiefs were abolished.
Together with Kan they were all killed by Yang Jian; their fiefs were abolished.
Preceding 與 and focus 衎並為 require a continuous 'together with Kan…' sense; 'Kan they were all' is ungrammatical and drops 與.
It is like arms used daily—hard to accomplish the enterprise below the ramparts;
It is like arms used daily—hard to accomplish the enterprise of Gaixia;
垓下 is the place-name Gaixia; generalizing to 'below the ramparts' loses the proper noun the idiomatic already keeps.
